Claude Is Not Your Intern. It Is Your GTM Operating System.

Strategy · AI

Most teams use Claude like a talented intern with amnesia.

They open a blank chat, paste a vague request, receive a competent answer, and start again the next day. The model never receives a durable picture of the company, the market, the customer, the sales process, or the standard by which good work should be judged.

The result is helpful output without organizational advantage.

Claude becomes substantially more useful when it is treated as a context-aware operating layer: a system that works from the same commercial source material, follows repeatable procedures, produces standard outputs, and knows when human approval is required.

Start with a GTM context pack

The foundation is not a clever prompt. It is a maintained set of company knowledge.

Create a concise context pack containing:

  1. Company definition: What the company does, for whom, and why it matters.

  2. Product truth: Current capabilities, limitations, integrations, roadmap boundaries, and prohibited claims.

  3. ICP definitions: Priority segments, buying triggers, stakeholders, exclusions, and disqualifiers.

  4. Positioning system: Purpose, elevator pitch, benefit statements, proof points, objections, and approved language.

  5. Commercial process: Pipeline stages, qualification criteria, required evidence, next-step standards, and handoffs.

  6. Voice guide: Tone, vocabulary, phrases to avoid, example writing, and channel differences.

  7. Competitive map: Alternatives, differentiators, known weaknesses, and how buyers frame the decision.

  8. Source policy: Approved internal sources, citation expectations, confidentiality rules, and verification requirements.

Keep each component short enough to maintain. A stale 80-page brand book is less useful than eight precise documents that reflect the current business.

Turn repeated work into named workflows

Once the context is stable, identify tasks the team performs repeatedly. Give each workflow a name, a required input, a sequence, a defined output, and an approval point.

Examples include:

  • Weekly Market Signal Brief

  • Priority Account Dossier

  • Sales Call Preparation Pack

  • Voice-of-Customer Analysis

  • Partner Opportunity Score

  • Founder Interview Content Pack

  • Campaign Postmortem

  • Competitive Change Alert

For a Priority Account Dossier, Claude should not merely "research Acme." The workflow should specify what matters: company priorities, current initiatives, relevant executives, likely problem, buying trigger, existing stack, partner overlap, risk factors, possible opening thesis, and sources requiring verification.

That consistency makes the output comparable across accounts and useful to a team.

Separate generation from decision-making

An operating system needs boundaries.

Claude can propose priority accounts; a commercial lead approves the prioritization. Claude can draft outbound language; the account owner verifies the premise and sends it. Claude can identify patterns in calls; the team decides whether those patterns justify repositioning. Claude can produce a campaign brief; a human approves claims, budget, and audience.

The principle is simple:

Automate preparation and pattern recognition before automating consequential decisions.

This keeps the system fast without allowing plausible but unverified output to enter the market as fact.

Connect the commercial loop

The highest-value design is not a collection of independent prompts. It is a loop.

Market research identifies a new buying signal. That signal changes account priority. Account conversations produce objections and language. Those conversations update the messaging system. The revised message informs content and campaigns. Campaign and pipeline performance create new evidence. The evidence updates the next market brief.

Claude can help maintain continuity across this loop because its role is not limited to drafting. It can compare new inputs with the established context, flag contradictions, identify missing evidence, and prepare the next decision.

Anthropic's own product direction reflects this shift: Projects, connectors, Skills, and agentic workflows increasingly organize models around reusable context and repeatable work rather than isolated chats.

The minimum viable Claude GTM system

A small company can begin with four components:

Monday: Claude assembles a market and account signal brief.

Before calls: It produces standardized preparation dossiers.

After calls: It converts notes into objections, next steps, CRM-ready fields, and messaging insights.

Friday: It summarizes what changed in the market, pipeline, and customer language, then recommends experiments for human review.

That alone can improve the quality and continuity of a small GTM team without pretending the model should operate the business autonomously.

The durable advantage is not access to Claude. Competitors have that too. The advantage is the company-specific context, operating procedures, and learning loop built around it.

lowob takeaway: Do not ask how to get more answers from Claude. Ask how company knowledge, repeatable workflows, and human decisions can compound through it.

Selected sources: Anthropic: Introducing Agent Skills; Anthropic: Claude integrations; Anthropic: Claude Projects
